summary: This informational document looks at IPv6 multihoming without Network Address Translation. IPv4 NAPT routers handle source address selection, next-hop choice, and optionally DNS, and this explores how IPv6 hosts can get similar benefits using other approaches.

eli5.summary: A house with two roads out needs to pick the right one. NAT used to do that quietly, and this looks at other ways to do it for IPv6.

questions: how to handle multiple prefixes in ipv6
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts select addresses and routes when connected to multiple networks.

tldr.problem: When an IPv6 host or small network connects to multiple upstream networks, each provider assigns a different address prefix. The host must then choose the right source address for each destination, pick the correct gateway, and use the right DNS server, or traffic fails.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes three common network scenarios and describes how DHCPv6-based policy distribution can help hosts make correct selections for source addresses, next hops, and DNS servers without using network address translation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC concludes that DHCPv6-based solutions are suitable for IPv6 multihoming; NPTv6 (IPv6-to-IPv6 NAT) may be needed as an interim solution for hosts that do not support the mechanisms described.

facts.label: Problem categories
facts.value: Source address selection, next-hop selection, DNS server selection

today: RFC 7157 is an Informational document published in March 2014. It remains relevant as IPv6 deployment continues. The DHCPv6-based solutions it recommends have been implemented and deployed, though broad adoption of multihoming-without-NAT solutions has been gradual. For hosts and networks that do not support the mechanisms, NPTv6 or traditional NAT remain interim options.

sections.title: The Problem with IPv6 Multihoming
sections.content:
IPv6 was designed to avoid Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) and preserve end-to-end transparency: each device has its own globally unique address, and hosts can communicate directly without a translator in the middle. However, when a host or small network connects to multiple upstream networks—each controlled by a different service provider—the host receives multiple IPv6 address prefixes, one from each provider. This creates three hard problems that NAPT routers solve automatically in IPv4:

The host must select the right source address for each outgoing packet. If it picks an address from the wrong provider, ingress filtering may block the packet. The host must choose the correct next-hop router to reach each destination. On a shared link with multiple routers, the host cannot know which router connects to which network. And the host must select the correct DNS recursive server when providers use split-horizon DNS, where different servers respond based on the source address of the query.
sections.eli5: A house connected to two different internet providers gets a phone number from each one. When someone calls, the house needs to answer on the right phone, tell the mailman which door to use, and ask the right information service.

sections.title: Three Common Network Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes three typical ways a host or small network can be multihomed:

Scenario 1: Shared link with multiple routers. Two or more routers sit on the same link as the hosts, each connected to a different service provider network. Each router advertises its own prefix. The host receives multiple addresses and sees both routers as valid defaults, but does not know which router to use for traffic to which destination.

Scenario 2: Single gateway router, multiple uplinks. One gateway router connects the hosts to multiple upstream networks through separate interfaces. The gateway advertises all the provider prefixes to the hosts. The hosts again have multiple addresses but need to know which traffic to send to the gateway, and the gateway must know how to forward traffic from the hosts.

Scenario 3: Multiple interfaces on the host. The host itself has two or more network interfaces, each connected to a different provider. Each interface receives a unique address prefix. The host must route traffic to the correct interface and select the appropriate source address for each destination.
sections.eli5: A house might have two doors opening onto different roads, one gateway with two internet pipes, or a multi-room house where each room can reach a different provider.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
Any solution to IPv6 multihoming without NAT must satisfy two key requirements. End-to-end transparency means hosts must not use network address translation; the solution must allow a host's own IPv6 addresses to remain visible on the public Internet. This preserves the ability to set up direct peer-to-peer connections and avoids the need for NAT traversal mechanisms in applications.

Scalability is critical in service provider networks where edge devices must manage thousands of customer sites. A solution cannot rely on sending periodic packets to each site; it must be passive and lightweight.
sections.eli5: The solution must let people see the house's real address (no translator box), and must work when the phone company manages thousands of houses.

sections.title: How DHCPv6 Policy Distribution Solves It
sections.content:
The RFC recommends a policy-based approach using DHCPv6 options to distribute rules from the network to the host. Rather than having the host guess, each service provider uses DHCP to tell the host: "For destinations in my network range, use my address as the source and my router as the next hop."

For source address selection, RFC 7078 defines a DHCPv6 option to carry an address selection policy table. This table tells the host how to rank its addresses, so it consistently chooses the right one. For next-hop selection, the host can receive routing information via Router Advertisements enhanced with more-specific routes, or via DHCPv6 options. For DNS server selection, RFC 6731 proposes a DHCPv6 option that pairs DNS recursive server addresses with domain suffixes, so the host knows which server to query for which domain.

This approach has an advantage over router discovery or dynamic routing protocols: DHCPv6 provides per-host configuration, avoiding the scaling and security issues of routers advertising policies to all hosts on a link.
sections.eli5: The internet provider tells the house, via its setup protocol, which address to use, which door to go out, and which information service to ask. The house remembers the rules and follows them.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges practical challenges in deploying a pure multihoming-without-NAT solution. Non-MHMP hosts (those that do not support the new mechanisms) may still exist. One option is for a gateway router to identify which hosts support multihoming and assign them multiple prefixes, while assigning a single prefix to legacy hosts and applying NPTv6 only to their traffic.

Coexistence between old and new hosts is possible: the gateway can treat them separately, or assign multiple prefixes to all hosts and perform selective NAT only on non-compliant traffic. In scenarios 1 and 3 with multiple routers or interfaces, legacy hosts can be placed behind a NAT box.

When multiple policy distributors exist, policy collision can occur: two providers send conflicting rules to the same host. The RFC notes that implementations must decide how to resolve conflicts, and consistency is needed to avoid interoperability issues. Some administrators may prioritize policies from one interface over others, or require a single representative provider to merge policies before distribution.
sections.eli5: Old computers might not understand the new rules. The gateway can give them a translator, or put them behind a special box. When two providers disagree about which rule to use, the house has to pick one.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Moving policy control from routers to hosts and DHCP servers introduces new security threats. A malicious DHCP server on one link could send the host an evil policy—for example, redirecting a host's traffic to a rogue router or causing DNS queries to go to a spoofed server. This could enable session hijacking, denial of service, or wiretapping.

An attacker could also use a fake policy to cause information leakage: if different hosts receive different policies, those differences reveal information about the host, aiding fingerprinting or tracking.

The RFC suggests mitigations: limiting policy acceptance to secure, authenticated channels (such as over IPSEC or on a trusted cellular network), using local-link-only communication restrictions, deploying DNSSEC to verify DNS responses, using ingress filtering at service provider routers to reject spoofed source addresses, and encrypting policy distribution to prevent policy leakage.
sections.eli5: A bad server could give the house wrong directions, send its mail to a thief, or copy its address to track it. The house should only trust rules from providers it knows, use locks on letters, and have the post office check the return address.
